title: Everyone Says Shanghai Fashion Week Is Rising. How Far Is It From Being a Mature Stage?
excerpt: "The Chinese market is unusual. It sits completely outside the normal range, and it has no fixed model of development."
body:
"The Chinese market is unusual. It sits completely outside the normal range, and it has no fixed model of development."

This year's Shanghai Fashion Week was a busy affair.

A year ago the British fashion curator Gemma A. Williams published *Fashion China*, an English-language book about Chinese independent designers. This season she came back to Shanghai Fashion Week and found a wave of new designers. "It's like an explosion — three times what it was before," Williams told QDaily.

Compared with the spring/summer 2016 season, the number of runway shows at the main Xintiandi venue held steady at around 50. Add the 10 children's-wear shows at the 800Show venue and the international-brand shows at Friendship Hall inside the Shanghai Exhibition Center, and the total came to 61. MODE, the trade fair where buyers place their orders, is now in its third edition and has a new name, MODE 3.0; the West Bund Art Center added Ontimeshow as a MODE satellite venue. The organizers also introduced a fashion-presentation platform, Labelhood, for the first time, staging 12 Presentation shows.

Some tickets to Labelhood, the Presentation platform Shanghai Fashion Week officially introduced this year, were open to the public: anyone who passed the organizers' screening got in free. On April 10, when the independent designer brand WMWM held its static exhibition, so many people showed up that the layout inside the hall had to be changed. The fabric originally set among the audience for people to touch was moved aside, and a barrier went up so that visitors could only look at the display from outside it.

Commercial brands and designers each got what they wanted. C.J.YAO and KFC launched a co-branded line, a hazy, dreamlike collection inspired by the chain. Disney turned up at fashion week too, doing co-branded collections with four brands at once — Ji Cheng, Han Lulu, Cindy Soong and Makin Ma. Diesel, part of the Genius Group, came as well, bought the opening slot in the international-brand lineup, and rode the buzz with large-scale digital advertising on Shanghai's Huaihai Road. JORYA, backed by LV Capital, bought the closing show. Even Business of Fashion, the media outlet backed by LVMH, partnered with Shanghai Fashion Week, becoming its official media partner for the first time.

![The LANYU show at the main venue](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123952LH5rknaisRWPep16.jpg-w600)

![The C.J.YAO and KFC co-branded collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021239534HeNX7xW16KVEazY.jpg-w600)

![The JI CHENG and Disney co-branded collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123953o6b2ZnBIJzvea0d1.jpg-w600)

All of this makes Shanghai Fashion Week's influence look bigger and bigger. Mario Boselli, honorary president of the National Chamber for Italian Fashion, who was appointed "fashion ambassador of Shanghai Fashion Week," lived up to the title: "If any emerging fashion week is going to succeed in the near future, it will be Shanghai."

For the global fashion industry, the standing of the four major fashion weeks — Paris, Milan, London and New York — remains unshakable. But over the past few decades a number of "regional cities of local significance and status" have begun holding city-themed "fashion weeks" of their own, and every so often one of them makes a run at the title of "the fifth fashion week."

Williams went to Georgia Fashion Week last year. Collins, the founder of Fashion Fringe, is more bullish on New Delhi Fashion Week in India. And we shouldn't forget Tokyo and Seoul.

What makes Shanghai different?

Tasha Liu, a co-founder of the Chinese concept store Dong Liang, has worked many times with Lyu Xiaolei, deputy secretary-general of the Shanghai Fashion Week organizing committee, and has never once heard Lyu talk about building "the fifth fashion week." Liu thinks the label is applied mostly by Shanghai Fashion Week's partners, who see huge potential in the city — some even call it New Paris.

Energy is one obvious measure.

"no.10/7" is a joint label from the Korean star Kim Junsu and the Korean designer Juyoung Lee. Misun Song, at the agency behind the brand, is bullish on the Chinese market. She has traveled to more than a dozen Chinese cities to do research, Shenyang and Nantong among them. She found the differences between Chinese cities striking, and that diversity is what drew her in.

"Young Koreans have a high level of taste, but it's remarkably uniform — everyone chases the same trending style at the same time." The Chinese market, she feels, has a far larger consumer base and a wider range of style preferences, which for her is an enormous draw. With this trip behind her she now plans to bring more Korean designer brands into China. "In short, I've spent three years preparing to enter this market."

Japan's moment, by comparison, seems to have passed. Tokyo Fashion Week's heyday ran from the 1980s to the early 2000s, which was also the peak of luxury consumption in Japan. The Japanese public was collectively obsessed with luxury goods, and for the first time the luxury conglomerates trained all their attention, with unusual unity, on a single consumer market.

That concentration of resources made Japan's fashion industry more mature, and Japanese style even fed back into American fashion. For the past 50 years what the Japanese have been doing is turning their obsession with American fashion into an industry: create a Japanese fashion that imitates America, then sell it back to America.

In 2005, the Japanese government, wanting to strengthen Tokyo Fashion Week's international influence, set up a dedicated Apparel Strategy Committee, and from October 2005 it organized spring/summer and autumn/winter shows every year as an official body. But before Japan holds its order-placing shows it waits for Paris Fashion Week's to finish first, so many independent brands don't show in Japan at all, and when they do the timing is late.

"Tokyo is withering," Zhou Huihui, founder of the K Point showroom, told QDaily. K Point represents 36 Japanese brands, and this was its fifth time at Shanghai Fashion Week. "The situation in Japan is that most designers rely on retail, not on showrooms like the ones at Shanghai Fashion Week."

Seoul Fashion Week is a formidable competitor. Korea has deep pockets, and Korea Fashion Week invites 25 times as many foreign journalists as Tokyo does. Seoul's fashion industry also has a peculiarity of its own: celebrities matter enormously. K-pop, fashion, models, designers, stars and fans all converge on the same runway.

Lorenzo Hadar runs H.Lorenzo, the globally known buyer boutique in Los Angeles. Every year he spends a stretch of time living in Tokyo.

"For my buying business, Milan Fashion Week is too old and too boring — there's nothing new there. If you're ranking them, Milan should be dropped from the 'four major fashion weeks,' and the order should be Paris, London, Shanghai and Seoul," Hadar told QDaily. He placed two orders at MODE this year, buying directly from Yun Fengsiru (SFDA) and Liu Lu (Fusionco). Opening Ceremony, another well-known overseas buyer boutique, took a liking to Peng Chen, Heydey, Atelier Rouge Pekin and Moto Guo, and is still in talks with them.

![Buyers and brands at the MODE trade fair](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123954lPf2GVnCzS5hDtdp.jpg-w600)

![A showroom rack at MODE](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123954BePyHAV1Kx0Enh9p.jpg-w600)

![Visitors browsing a MODE stand](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123955shb6Fv7KqPoUlcwk.jpg-w600)

![The scene at MODE](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123955Rx1J9S5WwsLVm8tg.jpg-w600)

Shanghai is indeed rising, but it may be too early to say how much weight it carries. At the very least, it needs to design a number of its weaknesses out of the system.

The most obvious one is that exhibitors aren't sorted at all — everything is put together in one place. The next is timing.

Buyers have only a few days at each fashion week, and they go where it is most worth going. Dong Liang completes 70 to 80 percent of its orders each year during the four major fashion weeks, without waiting for Shanghai. Unlike the four majors, which coordinate with one another in orderly fashion, the other city-themed fashion weeks often talk to each other very little. In the spring/summer 2015 season, Seoul Fashion Week, Tokyo Fashion Week and Shanghai Fashion Week all landed on overlapping dates.

Last season Hadar, busy shuttling between the fashion weeks of Seoul, Shanghai and Tokyo, missed "Dong Liang Day." Many other buyers missed the whole thing. "Almost none of the Chinese independent designers I know of show or run a showroom in Seoul or Tokyo, but some international buyers will choose Seoul or Tokyo when the dates clash. Those two fashion weeks are relatively more mature," Liu told QDaily.

The riskiest problem is that the designers aren't mature yet and are already rushing to serve a fast-growing market. A group of young designers back from studying abroad have started brands and, playing the part, price their clothes as high as established designer labels do. The fashion critic Lin Jian believes Chinese designers can perfectly well use the voice of the Chinese market to begin going mainstream.

"I often tell designers that a huge market is no excuse for shortchanging the product," Liu said.

These emerging designers all know by now that the domestic market is enormous, and some have started to speed up their diffusion lines. A diffusion line isn't necessarily the best choice for a designer — in 2015, Kate Spade shut its own down. Even so, in March, Masha Ma, which already has 10 stores in China, said it plans to open 100 across the mainland by 2022, concentrating on expanding her own label Ma by Ma, and will widen its product range by the end of the year with menswear and handbags.

"In Europe, new designers are more often encouraged to go to the big brands," Williams said. "Both paths work. But I still think emerging Chinese designers should work with big brands for at least three or four years, and then decide what they can do next — start their own brand, for instance."

![A designer's look on show at Dong Liang Day](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123956gp9rxjwW5mYzEo0h.jpg-w600)

![Garments on display at Dong Liang Day](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123956ywirhNZzQcBq2F4b.jpg-w600)

![Visitors at the Dong Liang Day exhibition](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702123957Cmy4k1W03wl972IT.jpg-w600)

![The static exhibition at this season's Dong Liang Day](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021239572ifAzMsO7TkEpVec.jpg-w600)

The silhouettes he saw most often this season, Hadar said, are ones Japanese designers were already making in the 1980s. His other point is that set against Japanese designers, Chinese designers have plenty to recommend them in the cut of their clothes, but the fabrics and the craftsmanship still need to improve.

"Making clothes isn't only about making clothes," Hadar said.

Should everyone wait for the designers to grow up? Or should the enthusiasm of consumers and partners in this huge market, and their hunger for "the fifth fashion week," be used to force things along as fast as possible? There is no settled answer.

At this season's "Haishang International Forum" during Shanghai Fashion Week, Carlo Capasa, president of the National Chamber for Italian Fashion, argued that Chinese designers should work more with the world's best photographers and stylists. He cited Burberry's styling and photography, and suggested designers measure themselves against that luxury brand. He also suggested that Chinese design position itself as accessible luxury. The chamber is currently discussing a commercial partnership with the Shanghai Fashion Week organizing committee.

Another view holds that if a designer brand's own image and creative work aren't mature yet, a better stylist won't save it.

"Personally I don't really agree with bringing the world's most famous stylists and photographers to Shanghai Fashion Week. I know a lot of people will say you have to align with international standards, learn more — and up to a point that really does matter. It's the same in Europe: the most successful photographers won't work with designers who are just starting out, unless you have some platform to bring them together," Williams said. The crux of it, she thinks, is that "the Chinese market is unusual. It sits completely outside the normal range, and it has no fixed model of development."

Neither the European and American fashion weeks nor Tokyo's, in fact, offer Shanghai much to copy. The first group has rich fashion soil built up over time; the second has a huge middle class and a domestic market already mature enough. That is why fashion in Japan and fashion in Europe and America grew so rich and yet so unlike each other. Last season Hadar said he remembered that even at Tokyo Fashion Week's peak, apart from the big names that had grown up in Europe, Japanese brands had no ambition to sell into Europe.

And yet this Los Angeles buyer boutique, out of admiration for Japanese designers' taste and the quality of their products, took them to the European and American markets anyway — and they were a hit.

Chinese designers face an entirely different environment. Behind them is a fashion consumer market that is huge, varied and fast-growing, and whose taste is still rudimentary. Even if consumers do become sophisticated one day, it will be the work of many countries' and many communities' fashion cultures acting on them at once. As the most mature window for that exchange, Shanghai Fashion Week is bound to refract the complexity, and it has to find what genuinely suits it.

Sara Maino, senior fashion editor at Italian Vogue and head of the emerging-designer program Vogue Talent, has been to Shanghai many times, but this was her first Shanghai Fashion Week. She didn't even watch the runway shows, moving instead between the trade fair and the showrooms, hoping to find more interesting designers.

The one show she did watch was C.J.YAO, and she thought it ran too long. "The designer may have put every idea she had into it. That doesn't make sense."
